question.text: Why is a crash with a commercial vehicle so dangerous for car occupants?

answer.text: Commercial vehicles are so large and heavy that they maneuver slowly, and car occupants are far more likely to be hurt or killed in a crash with one.

teaching.text: Size and weight make a truck slow to maneuver and deadly for the car in a crash. Remember: big, heavy, slow to maneuver.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Commercial vehicles are so large and heavy that they maneuver slowly, and car occupants are far more likely to be hurt or killed in a crash with one.

question.text: How do stopping distances compare for a car and a truck at highway speed?

answer.text: At fifty-five miles per hour a passenger vehicle stops in about one hundred thirty feet, while a commercial vehicle needs about four hundred feet.

teaching.text: Cutting in front of a truck takes away the long distance it needs to stop. Remember: one thirty versus four hundred.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At fifty-five miles per hour a passenger vehicle stops in about one hundred thirty feet, while a commercial vehicle needs about four hundred feet.

question.text: What are a truck's no zones, and why avoid them?

answer.text: Trucks have blind spots called no zones in front, beside and close behind them; lingering there hides you and raises the chance the truck hits you while turning or changing lanes.

teaching.text: Pass through a truck's blind spots instead of staying in them. Remember: no zones hide you.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Trucks have blind spots called no zones in front, beside and close behind them; lingering there hides you and raises the chance the truck hits you while turning or changing lanes.

question.text: Which headlights should you use at night behind a truck or bus?

answer.text: At night, use low beams when following a truck or bus.

teaching.text: High beams glare in a truck's big mirrors, so dim them. Remember: low beams behind trucks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night, use low beams when following a truck or bus.

question.text: How far should you follow a commercial vehicle?

answer.text: Keep well back from a commercial vehicle and never draft behind it, adding even more distance as weather or road conditions worsen.

teaching.text: A long gap lets you see around the truck and keeps you out of its blind spot. Remember: stay back, never draft.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep well back from a commercial vehicle and never draft behind it, adding even more distance as weather or road conditions worsen.

question.text: How much farther does a commercial vehicle need to stop than a car at highway speed?

answer.text: A car needs about one hundred thirty feet to stop from fifty-five miles per hour, but a commercial vehicle at that speed needs about four hundred feet.

teaching.text: A truck needs far more road to stop than a car at the same speed. Remember: trucks stop far longer.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A car needs about one hundred thirty feet to stop from fifty-five miles per hour, but a commercial vehicle at that speed needs about four hundred feet.

question.text: A truck ahead signals a right turn. What might it do, and where should you stop?

answer.text: A truck signaling a right turn may swing wide to the left first, so stop behind the white stop line or it may not be able to turn without hitting you.

teaching.text: The truck swings left to turn right, so leave it the room. Remember: trucks swing wide right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A truck signaling a right turn may swing wide to the left first, so stop behind the white stop line or it may not be able to turn without hitting you.

question.text: Why must you never cross behind a backing truck?

answer.text: Never cross behind a truck that is backing or about to back up, because a typical trailer, about eight and a half feet wide, can block a car from the driver's view.

teaching.text: If you cannot see the driver, the driver cannot see you behind the trailer. Remember: backing trailers hide cars.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never cross behind a truck that is backing or about to back up, because a typical trailer, about eight and a half feet wide, can block a car from the driver's view.

question.text: How should you merge onto and exit a freeway near trucks?

answer.text: Merging onto a freeway, match the traffic flow, pick your spot and go, since trucks may be unable to move over; when exiting, leave space ahead and signal early.

teaching.text: Trucks may not be able to move over, so merge decisively. Remember: match flow, pick, go.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Merging onto a freeway, match the traffic flow, pick your spot and go, since trucks may be unable to move over; when exiting, leave space ahead and signal early.

question.text: How should you signal and move around a truck?

answer.text: Signal lane changes and turns well ahead of a truck, and never cut it off or force it to slow or stop suddenly.

teaching.text: Early signals give the truck driver time; sudden moves take it away. Remember: signal early, never cut in.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signal lane changes and turns well ahead of a truck, and never cut it off or force it to slow or stop suddenly.

question.text: How do you pass a truck, and when may you pull back in?

answer.text: Pass commercial vehicles on the left at a steady speed, and pull back in only once the whole truck cab shows in your rearview mirror.

teaching.text: Wait to see the whole cab in your mirror before you move back. Remember: whole cab in mirror.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pass commercial vehicles on the left at a steady speed, and pull back in only once the whole truck cab shows in your rearview mirror.

question.text: What should you do while passing a truck?

answer.text: Stay visible to the truck driver while passing, allow enough time and distance, and keep both hands on the wheel against the truck's strong air draft.

teaching.text: A truck's air draft can push your car sideways as you pass. Remember: stay seen, hold the wheel.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stay visible to the truck driver while passing, allow enough time and distance, and keep both hands on the wheel against the truck's strong air draft.

question.text: What should you check before passing a truck with a trailer?

answer.text: Watch a truck's turn signals before passing it, especially one with a trailer that may swing left or right before turning and could force you off the road.

teaching.text: A trailer may swing before it turns, so read the signals first. Remember: watch the trailer's signals.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Watch a truck's turn signals before passing it, especially one with a trailer that may swing left or right before turning and could force you off the road.

question.text: How should you treat trucks in roundabouts?

answer.text: Avoid passing or driving beside trucks in roundabouts.

teaching.text: A truck may need more than one lane in a roundabout. Remember: never beside trucks in circles.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Avoid passing or driving beside trucks in roundabouts.

question.text: What should you do when a truck or bus passes you?

answer.text: Slow down when a truck or bus passes you, especially in bad weather, and turn on your wipers before its tire spray arrives.

teaching.text: Start your wipers before the spray, not after it hits. Remember: slow down, wipers on.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Slow down when a truck or bus passes you, especially in bad weather, and turn on your wipers before its tire spray arrives.

question.text: Which vehicles count as slow-moving vehicles?

answer.text: Slow-moving vehicles cannot go faster than twenty-five miles per hour and include Amish buggies, combines, tractors towing wagons, and industrial or construction equipment; four-wheelers and golf carts do not count.

teaching.text: Farm and construction equipment and buggies count; carts and four-wheelers do not. Remember: buggies and combines, not carts.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Slow-moving vehicles cannot go faster than twenty-five miles per hour and include Amish buggies, combines, tractors towing wagons, and industrial or construction equipment; four-wheelers and golf carts do not count.

question.text: How do you recognize a slow-moving vehicle, and how should you act?

answer.text: A slow-moving vehicle carries an orange triangle on its back, and its driver will usually pull aside when possible, so stay patient.

teaching.text: Slow vehicles usually pull aside when they can, so wait patiently. Remember: orange triangle, stay patient.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A slow-moving vehicle carries an orange triangle on its back, and its driver will usually pull aside when possible, so stay patient.

question.text: How should you follow a horse and rider or a buggy?

answer.text: Behind a horse and rider or a horse-drawn buggy, slow to fifteen to twenty miles per hour and keep at least twenty feet back, and never honk or rev the engine.

teaching.text: A startled horse can bolt, so slow down, stay back and stay quiet. Remember: slow, back, and quiet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Behind a horse and rider or a horse-drawn buggy, slow to fifteen to twenty miles per hour and keep at least twenty feet back, and never honk or rev the engine.

question.text: How does a slow vehicle's top speed compare with the speed for following a horse?

answer.text: Slow-moving vehicles top out at twenty-five miles per hour, but when following a horse you slow further, to fifteen to twenty miles per hour, and stay twenty feet back.

teaching.text: Twenty-five is a slow vehicle's top; fifteen to twenty is your speed behind a horse. Remember: slower still behind horses.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Slow-moving vehicles top out at twenty-five miles per hour, but when following a horse you slow further, to fifteen to twenty miles per hour, and stay twenty feet back.

question.text: Whom must you always yield to on foot or on wheels like skateboards?

answer.text: Always yield to pedestrians, including walkers, joggers, hikers, skateboarders and people pushing strollers, and take every precaution to avoid hitting one.

teaching.text: Anyone on foot or on a skateboard or stroller gets the right of way. Remember: always yield to pedestrians.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Always yield to pedestrians, including walkers, joggers, hikers, skateboarders and people pushing strollers, and take every precaution to avoid hitting one.

question.text: Where should you watch for pedestrians?

answer.text: Watch for pedestrians at driveways and alleys, stop signs, signals, roundabouts, crosswalks and intersections, and midblock even near a crosswalk.

teaching.text: People can step out at driveways, alleys, corners and midblock. Remember: pedestrians appear everywhere.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Watch for pedestrians at driveways and alleys, stop signs, signals, roundabouts, crosswalks and intersections, and midblock even near a crosswalk.

question.text: Must you yield to people crossing when your light is green?

answer.text: Even on a green light you must yield to people crossing.

teaching.text: Green lets you go only after people crossing are clear. Remember: green still means yield.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Even on a green light you must yield to people crossing.

question.text: A car ahead has stopped for a pedestrian. May you pass it?

answer.text: Never pass a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian, and take special care when a large truck or bus is stopped because it can hide a pedestrian.

teaching.text: A stopped car may be hiding someone about to step into your lane. Remember: never pass a stopped car.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never pass a vehicle stopped for a pedestrian, and take special care when a large truck or bus is stopped because it can hide a pedestrian.

question.text: Where there is no sidewalk, which way should pedestrians walk?

answer.text: Where there is no sidewalk, pedestrians walking along the road should face oncoming traffic, so watch both sides of the road.

teaching.text: Without sidewalks, walkers may be coming toward you on your side. Remember: walkers face traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Where there is no sidewalk, pedestrians walking along the road should face oncoming traffic, so watch both sides of the road.

question.text: Who needs extra time to cross the street?

answer.text: Give older people, young children and people with disabilities extra time to cross.

teaching.text: Signal timing does not change how fast some people can walk. Remember: give extra crossing time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Give older people, young children and people with disabilities extra time to cross.

question.text: What must you do for a pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog?

answer.text: The law requires you to stop or yield for a pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog, and you should not honk or rev the engine, which masks sounds they rely on.

teaching.text: Honking or revving drowns out the sounds a blind walker relies on. Remember: white cane: stop, stay quiet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The law requires you to stop or yield for a pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog, and you should not honk or rev the engine, which masks sounds they rely on.

question.text: Where must you stop at a crosswalk, and what must you never do?

answer.text: Michigan law requires stopping at the marked crosswalk limit line, or before the intersection if there is none, and you must never block a crosswalk.

teaching.text: Stop at the limit line and leave the crosswalk open. Remember: never block a crosswalk.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Michigan law requires stopping at the marked crosswalk limit line, or before the intersection if there is none, and you must never block a crosswalk.

question.text: What are mid-block crosswalks, and what may show where to stop?

answer.text: Mid-block crosswalks let pedestrians cross away from intersections, and a yield line sometimes shows drivers where to stop for them.

teaching.text: Crossings can be away from corners, sometimes with a yield line. Remember: mid-block crossings exist.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Mid-block crosswalks let pedestrians cross away from intersections, and a yield line sometimes shows drivers where to stop for them.

question.text: Where should you take special care for children?

answer.text: Take special care near parked cars, school zones, playgrounds and parks, where children can dart into the street.

teaching.text: Children can dart out from between parked cars without looking. Remember: watch for darting children.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Take special care near parked cars, school zones, playgrounds and parks, where children can dart into the street.

question.text: Why are crashes with riders so serious?

answer.text: Motorcycles, scooters, mopeds and bicycles are hard to see and their speed and distance hard to judge, and a crash with a larger vehicle almost always injures or kills the rider.

teaching.text: Riders are easy to miss and badly hurt in any crash. Remember: riders are hard to see.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Motorcycles, scooters, mopeds and bicycles are hard to see and their speed and distance hard to judge, and a crash with a larger vehicle almost always injures or kills the rider.

question.text: How should you pass a motorcycle or bicycle rider?

answer.text: Give riders room and pass them like any other vehicle, by moving into the next lane when safe and legal; riders themselves are allowed to share a lane.

teaching.text: Use the next lane to pass a rider, the same as for a car. Remember: pass riders like cars.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Give riders room and pass them like any other vehicle, by moving into the next lane when safe and legal; riders themselves are allowed to share a lane.

question.text: Where are crashes with riders most likely?

answer.text: Intersections are among the riskiest places for crashes with riders, and drivers often tell police they never saw the motorcyclist.

teaching.text: At intersections, drivers often never see the rider at all. Remember: intersections are riskiest.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Intersections are among the riskiest places for crashes with riders, and drivers often tell police they never saw the motorcyclist.

question.text: Before turning left, how should you judge an oncoming rider?

answer.text: Before turning left, assume an oncoming rider is closer than they look and wait for them to pass.

teaching.text: A small vehicle coming toward you is nearer and faster than it seems. Remember: closer than they look.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before turning left, assume an oncoming rider is closer than they look and wait for them to pass.

question.text: How far should you follow a motorcyclist or bicyclist?

answer.text: Tailgating is illegal; leave at least three or four seconds behind a motorcyclist, scooter operator or bicyclist, who can stop shorter and may swerve for potholes or rail crossings.

teaching.text: Riders stop short and swerve for potholes, so leave a long gap. Remember: three or four seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Tailgating is illegal; leave at least three or four seconds behind a motorcyclist, scooter operator or bicyclist, who can stop shorter and may swerve for potholes or rail crossings.

question.text: How can a fast vehicle's wind affect a rider?

answer.text: A fast vehicle's wind blast can startle a rider or push them off balance, raising the chance of a crash.

teaching.text: Passing close can unbalance a rider even without contact. Remember: wind blast topples riders.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A fast vehicle's wind blast can startle a rider or push them off balance, raising the chance of a crash.

question.text: What clues suggest a rider is about to turn?

answer.text: A rider moving to one side of the lane, checking over a shoulder, or leaning the vehicle is probably about to turn, in addition to any turn or hand signal you see.

teaching.text: A lean, a glance back or a lane shift means a turn is coming. Remember: lean, look, shift sides.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A rider moving to one side of the lane, checking over a shoulder, or leaning the vehicle is probably about to turn, in addition to any turn or hand signal you see.

question.text: Why can a rider's light be hard to pick out?

answer.text: A rider's single headlight or taillight can blend into the lights of other traffic, so look carefully.

teaching.text: One small light is easy to lose among car lights. Remember: single lights blend in.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A rider's single headlight or taillight can blend into the lights of other traffic, so look carefully.

question.text: When should you check your blind spot for a rider?

answer.text: Before changing lanes and again after passing, check your blind spot for a rider and be sure you can see them clearly in the rearview mirror before moving back.

teaching.text: Check for riders before you change lanes and again after you pass. Remember: check before and after.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before changing lanes and again after passing, check your blind spot for a rider and be sure you can see them clearly in the rearview mirror before moving back.

question.text: Why is opening your car door into traffic dangerous?

answer.text: Opening a car door into the path of approaching traffic, including motorcycles and bicycles, is dangerous and illegal; check mirrors and open the door with your right hand.

teaching.text: Look back before your door swings into a rider's path. Remember: look before opening doors.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Opening a car door into the path of approaching traffic, including motorcycles and bicycles, is dangerous and illegal; check mirrors and open the door with your right hand.

question.text: May you drive beside or pass a motorcyclist in the same lane?

answer.text: It is illegal for a motorist to drive beside a motorcyclist or pass one within the same lane; use the adjacent lane when legal and safe.

teaching.text: A motorcycle gets the whole lane, just like a car. Remember: never share a motorcycle's lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: It is illegal for a motorist to drive beside a motorcyclist or pass one within the same lane; use the adjacent lane when legal and safe.

question.text: Where do most vehicle and motorcycle crashes happen?

answer.text: Most vehicle-motorcycle crashes happen at intersections and on busy city streets.

teaching.text: Busy city streets and intersections are where most motorcycle crashes happen. Remember: intersections and busy streets.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most vehicle-motorcycle crashes happen at intersections and on busy city streets.

question.text: Which motorcycles may use freeways?

answer.text: Motorcycles with engines of one hundred twenty-five cubic centimeters or more may legally use freeways and limited-access highways.

teaching.text: Engine size decides which motorcycles may use freeways. Remember: bigger engines on freeways.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Motorcycles with engines of one hundred twenty-five cubic centimeters or more may legally use freeways and limited-access highways.

question.text: How can a motorcycle's size fool your judgment?

answer.text: A motorcycle's single headlight and small profile can make it seem farther away and slower than it is, a risk that grows at night and in bad weather.

teaching.text: Give yourself extra margin when judging a motorcycle's gap. Remember: closer and faster than seen.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A motorcycle's single headlight and small profile can make it seem farther away and slower than it is, a risk that grows at night and in bad weather.

question.text: Why might a motorcycle slow without brake lights?

answer.text: Motorcyclists often slow by engine braking and downshifting, which does not light the brake lights, so keep extra space, and use your horn sparingly so you do not startle riders.

teaching.text: A rider may slow down with no brake light at all. Remember: engine braking, no brake light.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Motorcyclists often slow by engine braking and downshifting, which does not light the brake lights, so keep extra space, and use your horn sparingly so you do not startle riders.

question.text: What makes a vehicle a moped under Michigan law?

answer.text: Under Michigan law a moped has two or three wheels, an engine of no more than one hundred cubic centimeters, a top speed of no more than thirty miles per hour on level ground, and no gear shifting by the rider.

teaching.text: A moped is small, slow and shifts no gears. Remember: small engine, low speed, no shifting.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Under Michigan law a moped has two or three wheels, an engine of no more than one hundred cubic centimeters, a top speed of no more than thirty miles per hour on level ground, and no gear shifting by the rider.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: small engine, low speed, no shifting

question.text: What does the word scooter cover?

answer.text: Scooter is a general term covering mopeds and also more powerful two-wheelers that fall outside the moped definition.

teaching.text: Not every scooter is a moped; some are more powerful. Remember: scooter is the broad term.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Scooter is a general term covering mopeds and also more powerful two-wheelers that fall outside the moped definition.

question.text: What is an autocycle?

answer.text: An autocycle is a three-wheeled motorcycle with safety belts, a roll bar or hoops and a steering wheel but no straddle seat, and it deserves the same watchfulness as a motorcycle.

teaching.text: An autocycle gets the same care as a motorcycle. Remember: three wheels, steering wheel.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: An autocycle is a three-wheeled motorcycle with safety belts, a roll bar or hoops and a steering wheel but no straddle seat, and it deserves the same watchfulness as a motorcycle.

question.text: Where may bicyclists ride in Michigan?

answer.text: Bicyclists may ride on any Michigan road except limited-access freeways, anywhere in the lane as long as they ride with traffic, with the same rights and duties as motorists.

teaching.text: Bicyclists have the same rights and duties as drivers on most roads. Remember: bikes ride with traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicyclists may ride on any Michigan road except limited-access freeways, anywhere in the lane as long as they ride with traffic, with the same rights and duties as motorists.

question.text: What should you look for before turning right or pulling off the road?

answer.text: Before turning right or pulling off the road, look for bicyclists coming up from behind on the shoulder or in a bike lane, and let them pass first when appropriate.

teaching.text: Look behind for riders before every right turn. Remember: check for bikes behind.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before turning right or pulling off the road, look for bicyclists coming up from behind on the shoulder or in a bike lane, and let them pass first when appropriate.

question.text: May you use a bike lane as a right-turn lane?

answer.text: Never use a bike lane as a right-turn lane, and do not pass a bicyclist and then turn right in front of them unless it is safe.

teaching.text: Passing a rider and then turning across them is a common crash. Remember: bike lanes are not turn lanes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never use a bike lane as a right-turn lane, and do not pass a bicyclist and then turn right in front of them unless it is safe.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: bike lanes are not turn lanes

question.text: How much space must you give when passing a bicyclist?

answer.text: Michigan law requires at least three feet of space when passing a bicyclist; if that is impractical, pass at a safe distance and speed, and some cities require five feet.

teaching.text: Give at least three feet, and five where a city requires it. Remember: three feet when passing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Michigan law requires at least three feet of space when passing a bicyclist; if that is impractical, pass at a safe distance and speed, and some cities require five feet.

question.text: May you pass a bicyclist in a no-passing zone?

answer.text: You may pass a bicyclist in a no-passing zone if it is safe, and after passing stay out of the lane until well clear; large vehicles and oversized loads need even more room.

teaching.text: A bicyclist may be passed in a no-passing zone when it is safe. Remember: safe pass allowed, then clear.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You may pass a bicyclist in a no-passing zone if it is safe, and after passing stay out of the lane until well clear; large vehicles and oversized loads need even more room.

question.text: Must bicyclists ride in the bike lane?

answer.text: Bicyclists are not required to ride in a bike lane and may leave it to turn left or avoid hazards.

teaching.text: A rider leaving the bike lane to turn or dodge a hazard is within the rules. Remember: bike lanes are optional.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicyclists are not required to ride in a bike lane and may leave it to turn left or avoid hazards.

question.text: Why are recumbent bikes and handcycles easy to miss?

answer.text: Low three-wheeled recumbent bikes and handcycles are hard to see despite mirrors and tall orange flags.

teaching.text: Look low as well as high for riders. Remember: low riders, hard to see.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Low three-wheeled recumbent bikes and handcycles are hard to see despite mirrors and tall orange flags.
